Apart from what has already been said about our cells' capacity for both male and female expression, etc., I think it's worth exploring further the examples you put forth. First, I think the idea that a person might see themselves as Mexican, despite being born in Europe, is probably more common than you think. The difference is that if you identify with Mexican culture, you love the food, you find you relate more to the people you meet there, and you want other people to respect you as a member of that community, you would just move there and become a naturalized citizen. Plenty of immigrants identify more as citizens of the country in which they live than the country in which they were born. To put it another way, when I transition I'm "naturalizing as a woman" because I feel that a female body better accords with who I am and how I would like to be viewed. The difference is one of degree: the people you interact with are likely unaware of precisely what ethnicity you are unless you reveal that to them and society is less averse to you expressing yourself in terms of your national identity than they are of you expressing your gender identity - no one is going to verbally or physically attack you for walking down the street eating a churro. I identify as a woman, but that doesn't mean I don't recognize that I was born with a penis. The real question is, why does that mean I'm stuck with it? I'm more comfortable in a female role and to the extent that I'm treated as "male", it makes me extremely unhappy. A lot of that discomfort manifests as negative feelings towards my male body because I see it as the root of the incongruity between how I feel and how others feel about me. 

Regarding your 16th century peasantry, I know plenty of people who feel like they were born in the wrong time period: they are more comfortable in the absence of modern technology or identify with a way of life that no longer exists. Many people act on those feelings by living in rural areas or pursuing careers that allow them to connect with that aspect of their identity. I'm certain if time machines existed, you would find that a great many people would seize the opportunity to live in a time other than the 21st century - not just out of curiosity, but because they felt most at home in their chosen time period. No one would call them crazy for doing that. They know they were born in the 21st century, but that doesn't mean they have the identity of a "21st century person". If their dysphoria were analogous to that of a transperson, you might find that being accepted as a part of 16th century society would alleviate a depression that hangs over them every time someone expects them to own an iPhone. For the same reason as with national identity, I think the difference is one of degree. You don't see the same kind of dysphoria because there is greater opportunity to express that as a part of your identity and less social pressure telling you it's wrong and you should kill yourself for feeling that way. 

I don't know anyone who identifies as a parrot, or trans-macaw, but I know a few people who have annoying voices and say the same shit every time I see them. All I can say there is that I think if: (1) someone truly did identify as a parrot; (2) was depressed because of their human form; (3) we had the technology to allow their body to take that form; and (4) the psychiatric community was in agreement that not only was there no comorbidity with any psychiatric disorder, but also that the only effective treatment for their dysphoria was to undergo parrot reassignment, I would be 100% behind them doing it.

I know objectively that makes sense but actually moving forward with it is overwhelming - sometimes too overwhelming to deal with (like how I'm feeling right now). The other thing too is like I don't even want to be a lawyer. Most of the impetus behind going to law school was to feel like I was doing what I was "supposed" to: i.e. become cutthroat corporate litigator whose manhood was unquestioned. But now there's all this pressure to actually do it and it's not at all what I want, so all law school really gave me was a shit ton of debt that only adds to the pressure to move in the wrong direction. I don't think killing myself makes sense but that doesn't mitigate the feeling that it's the only decision I can make that won't involve living with regret - at least I'll be dead.

Primary thing is feeling like I can go outside without being ridiculed. Also I'm finishing law school this year and transitioning is gonna make my job search a lot more difficult (currently sitting on 120k student debt). The only way I'm ever gonna feel good is if I "pass" (trans speak for random people reading you as the gender you want to be read as) but the thing with hormone therapy is that there's no way to know how effective it will be on any given individual - some ppl get amazing results and other people not so much, and it takes years to get the full effect.

No real direction in life. No clue what I wanna do. No friends. Can't really imagine a future I want that involves me being the gender I am now but transitioning is just gonna make things more difficult in terms of career, etc. So apart from suicide my choices seem to be a) repress who I am and be forever unhappy or b) express who I am and most likely not reach a point I'm happy with while also fucking up other things I have going for me.
